Clinical Safety with Artificial Intelligence Depends on Clinicians Questioning Model Outputs

In a perspective published in Discover Artificial Intelligence, researchers emphasize that the safe clinical use of artificial intelligence may depend less on model performance and more on a clinician’s ability to evaluate model outputs. Large language models are increasingly used across various clinical settings to support clinical reasoning and decision-making. Although early studies suggest these systems have demonstrated strong performance on medical knowledge and reasoning tasks with the potential to reduce medical errors, emerging evidence also highlights significant safety concerns. Specifically, artificial intelligence outputs can contain clinically significant management errors that are not readily apparent to users, leaving open the central question of how to integrate these tools into practice to consistently improve patient outcomes.

The authors, Ryan W. Hunton, Tama The, and Jonathan Ilgen, argue that AI-assisted reasoning must be examined as an unfolding sequence of decisions rather than an isolated single moment. This multi-stage interaction begins with the initial choice of whether to consult artificial intelligence for a given clinical question. The process then progresses through determining how to engage with the tool, deciding how to interpret its resulting output, and finally determining whether to act upon the guidance provided in a clinical case.

According to the analysis, each stage in this sequence introduces distinct points of vulnerability and potential failure. Clinicians face risks that include inappropriate tool selection, providing incomplete or biased inputs, exhibiting overconfidence in fluent responses, and failing to recognize underlying errors or appreciate clinical nuance. Furthermore, these vulnerabilities are shaped by the same clinician factors that govern clinical reasoning more broadly, such as medical experience, clinical workload, and how healthcare providers handle uncertainty in practice.

Recognizing that AI-clinician collaboration functions as a continuous process reveals key opportunities for targeted medical training. The authors conclude that safe clinical implementation depends not merely on advancing model quality, but on cultivating the clinician’s ability to critically assess model responses. Preparing clinicians to identify when algorithmic outputs must be questioned, verified, or entirely set aside will be crucial as automated reasoning tools become more deeply embedded in routine patient care.

Subject of Research: Clinical uncertainty and decision-making during clinician interactions with artificial intelligence

Article Title: The arc of uncertainty across clinicians’ interactions with AI

Article References: Hunton, R. W., The, T., & Ilgen, J. (2026). The arc of uncertainty across clinicians’ interactions with AI. Discover Artificial Intelligence, 6(1), Article 1936. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44163-026-02851-3

Keywords: artificial intelligence, large language models, clinical reasoning, decision-making, clinical safety, management errors, uncertainty management, model verification, clinician training, medical education, tool selection, patient outcomes, fluent responses, clinical workload, decision sequence, medical error reduction, output interpretation
